<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par156 />{{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=15|verse=18}} {{GHGheb|text=וְלֹא כִחֲדוּ}}); {{GHGheb|text=בְּלִי חָשָׂ֑ךְ}} (prop. ''he restrains not'') ''unceasingly'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=14|verse=6}}; {{GHGheb|text=בַּל־יִמּוֹט}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=41|verse=15}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=93|verse=1}} {{GHGheb|text=בַּל־תִּמִּוֹט}}) and {{GHGheb|text=לֹא יִמּוֹט}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=40|verse=20}} (''without tottering'') ''immovably''; cf. also {{GHGheb|text=לֹא אֶמְעָ֑ד|translate=without wavering}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=26|verse=1}}.<section end=par156 />

<section begin=par157 />{{GHGpar-heading|157|Object-Clauses (Oratio Obliqua)}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|157|a}}
Clauses which depend on a transitive verb, especially on what are called {{GHGterm|verba cordis}}, i.e. verbs denoting any mental act, such as ''to see, to hear, to know, to perceive, to believe, to remember, to forget, to say, to think'', &c., may be subordinated to the governing verb without the help of a conjunction by simple juxtaposition ({{GHGpar|120|a}}), or they may be co-ordinated with it either with or without {{GHGterm|wāw copulative}} ({{GHGpar|120|d}}–h). As a rule, however, the objective clause is introduced by the conjunction {{GHGheb|text=כִּי|translate=that}}, less frequently by {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר|translate=that}}.<ref>On these clauses with {{GHGheb|text=כִּי}} and {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} and generally on clauses which we should render as subordinate, cf. P. Dörwald ‘Zur hebr. Syntax’ in ''Neue Jahrbb. für Philol. und Pädag.'' 1890, p. 115 ff.</ref>

Examples:—

(''a'') Object-clauses without a conjunction. Besides the passages mentioned in § 120 (especially under ''e'') there are a number of examples, in which a clause depending on a {{GHGterm|verbum dicendi}} or ''sentiendi'' (the ''oratio obliqua'' of the Latin and English Grammar) is added in the form of an independent noun-clause or verbal-clause; e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=12|verse=13}} {{GHGheb|text=אִמְרִי־נָא אֲחֹ֫תִי אָ֑תְּ|translate=say, I pray thee, thou}} art ''my sister''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=10|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=25|verse=3}}''<sup>a</sup>''<sup>.14</sup>, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=6|verse=6}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=8|verse=23}} (after {{GHGheb|text=שָׁמַע}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=9|verse=21}} (after {{GHGheb|text=יָדַע}}); verbal-clauses, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=50|verse=21}} ''thou thoughtest'' {{GHGheb|text=הֱיֽוֹת־אְהְיֶה כָמ֫וֹךָ|translate=I was surely like thyself}} [but read {{GHGheb|text=הָיוֹ}} for {{GHGheb|text=הֱיוֹת}}]; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=41|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=9|verse=48}} ''what ye have seen me do''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=48|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=7|verse=2}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|157|b}}
(''b'') Object-clauses introduced by {{GHGheb|text=כִּי}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=6|verse=5}} {{GHGheb|text=וַיַּרְא יְהֹוָה כִּי רַבָּה רָעַת הָֽאָדָם|translate=and the Lord saw that the wickedness of man was great}}, &c.—Direct narration also is very frequently introduced by {{GHGheb|text=כִּי}} (analogous to the ὅτι ''recitativum''; frequently, indeed, with the secondary idea of a particle of asseveration, as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=26|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=20|hidebook=1}}), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=21|verse=30}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=22|verse=16|hidebook=1}} f., 26:22, 29:32, 37:35, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=2|verse=24}}, &c., even when the direct narration is not expressly indicated, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=32|verse=31|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=41|verse=51|hidebook=1}} f., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=18|verse=4}}.—On the expression of a second object by means of a clause introduced by {{GHGheb|text=כִּי}}, see {{GHGpar|117|h}}.<ref>Instead of a complete objective clause we sometimes find a kind of accusative and infinitive construction, especially after {{GHGheb|text=נָתַן}} (prop. ''to give up'') in the sense of ''to allow'', e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=21|verse=23}} {{GHGheb|text=וְלֹֽא־נָתַן סִיחֹן אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵל עֲבֹר בִּגְבֻלוֹ|translate=and Sihon did not suffer Israel to pass through his border}}; 20:21; followed by an infinitive with {{GHGheb|text=לְ}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=20|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=7|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=3|verse=19}}.—Cf. also the analogous examples in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=28|verse=56}} (after {{GHGheb|text=נִסָּה|translate=to venture}}; see {{GHGpar|113|d}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=11|verse=20}} (after{{GHGheb|text=הָֽאֱמִין|translate=to trust}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=19|verse=4}} (after {{GHGheb|text=שָׁאַל|translate=to request}}).</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|157|c}}
(''c'') Object-clauses introduced by {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Est|chapter=3|verse=4}} {{GHGheb|text=כִּֽי־הִגִּיד לָהֶם אֲשֶׁר־הוּא יְהוּדִי|translate=for he had told them that he was a Jew}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=18|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=20|verse=26}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=8|verse=12}},<ref>In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=28|verse=9}} a ''subject''-clause is thus introduced by {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} instead of the usual {{GHGheb|text=כִּי}}.</ref> even before direct narration, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=15|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=1|verse=4}}. Somewhat frequently {{GHGheb|text=אֲשְׁר}} is preceded by<section end=par157 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>
